first, the phenomena of the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandhāyatana-dhātu*);
second, the phenomena of the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-samudaya*).
Third is the matter of the truths;
fourth is the matter of realized wisdom;
fifth is the matter of specific counteractive measures.
Sixth is the matter of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the matter of the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*), it is based on the inquiry concerning "self" and "mine.

Regarding the matter of the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-samudaya*), it is based on inquiry according to the forward order (*anuloma*) and inquiry according to the reverse order (*pratiloma*); that is, inquiry by way of arising (*utpāda*) and inquiry by way of cessation (*nirodha*), as well as inquiry by way of what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*).
Regarding that inquiry into the collection of causes and conditions, arising and ceasing are themselves the possible and the impossible (*sthāna-asthāna*).
As it is said in the Sūtra: "If one practices various virtues through bodily and verbal actions and yet is born in the evil realms, such a thing is impossible."

Regarding the basis of the truths (*satya-vastu*), there is the forward progression of dependent origination (*anuloma-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the reverse progression of dependent origination (*pratiloma-pratītyasamutpāda*).

As for the forward progression of dependent origination, the two truths constitute the essence of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) because they possess both cause and fruit, being the very substance of the phenomena of outflowing conditioned formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra-dharma*).

Regarding the collection of adverse causes and conditions: the pure essence of the two truths can be extinguished by relying on the Path; therefore, the Truth of the Path is called the Truth of Cessation.
Thus, based on these two pairs of truths, the questions concerning defilement and purity are posed.
Based on the nature of defiled phenomena according to the two kinds of truths, there is the question concerning the world of birth and death;
based on the nature of purified phenomena according to the two kinds of truths, there is the question concerning quiescent nirvāṇa.

Thus, one is born into the world in this sequence and transcends the world to attain nirvāṇa; such is the distinction between the two types—the worldly and the nirvanic—based upon nirvāṇa with remainder and nirvāṇa without remainder.
It should be understood that when such questions regarding the world and other matters are asked based on ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), this is their intended meaning.
For this reason, the fourfold categories based on truth refute the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Regarding "based on the matter of realized knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna-vastu*): it refers to questions concerning what is to be known and what is to be abandoned, and questions concerning what is to be attained and what is to be cultivated.

Following this sequence, that knowledge receives the name "knowledge" (*jñāna*) at the time of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). For one who has already realized knowledge, from this point onward, it receives the name "path of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Thus, based on that realization, there are questions concerning realized knowledge.
One should understand this meaning: that which is called "attaining wisdom" is named "practice.

This is because one attains the fruit of the supramundane right path by abandoning that accumulation, and because one abandons the body of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*); thus, the question is posed based on the abandonment of those things.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Therefore, Jālinīprabha!

To ask about that which is without attainment and without grasping, without realization and without discrimination, without knowledge and without dependence, and without cultivation and without the view of cultivation—that is the correct question."
What does this clarify?

Within *tathatā* (suchness), regarding the words and phrases as they have been spoken, it is said that there is no such cognition; this is to exclude the existence of such phenomena in that place. Just as in each instance where a phrase is analyzed, one also excludes the existence of such [a phenomenon] in each individual part of that phrase.
"Non-appropriation" means not falsely discriminating that "I have attained.
"Non-discrimination" means not falsely discriminating that "I have realized."
"Non-reliance" means that one does not falsely discriminate, thinking "I have already realized nirvāṇa.
This non-discrimination is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

As for the term "reliance," it refers to relying upon the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because it is taught that the path of seeing serves as the basis for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
There is no one who sees through cultivation, because one does not see a self cultivating the path.
To teach the Dharma in this way is called "correct.
That which relies upon the objects of counteraction refers to phenomena such as the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Unwholesome phenomena are termed "opposites" in relation to wholesome phenomena, serving as their antidotes.
Furthermore, those wholesome phenomena are distinguished by two types, namely the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that all non-Buddhists possess the fault of being shrouded in the long night of the turbidity of false views.
There are also two kinds of distinctions regarding the absence of such faults: namely, the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are distinguished by two types: namely, the distinction between the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*lokottara*).

Regarding these, there is a question concerning the activity of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) that treats its respective object of abandonment (*vipakṣa*), based on both conceptualization (*savikalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).
“Jālinīprabha!
If a bodhisattva perceives neither duality nor non-duality, they perceive neither the number two nor the number one, because they have negated the selfhood of graspable phenomena.”

Regarding the statement, "The question concerning the practice of equality in which ignorance is signless is called a correct question": this is because it takes up the characteristics of those phenomena in order to negate the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped.
Furthermore, regarding the question of "the practice of the equality of signlessness and signlessness," it is intended to negate the characteristics of both the speaker and the spoken.
Moreover, the "speaker" is termed "equality," while the "spoken" is termed "signs"; this is because all phenomena are known to be equal.
That which can be taught as the Dharma is also called "equality," because various types of dharmas are spoken of under the same name.

Regarding the matters of the Buddha’s Dharma: it relies on the Buddha, relies on the Dharma, relies on practice, relies on the locus, relies on the sentient beings to be converted, and relies on the realization of wisdom through progress; thus, the Buddha and others manifest these in successive order. Because of these distinctions, the questions are asked.
The various aspects of the Buddha and so forth should be understood.
"The various aspects of the Buddha" refers to the distinctions of time, family, clan, and lifespan.
"The various aspects of the Dharma" refers to the distinctions of the sūtras, geyas, and so forth.
The variety of the Saṃgha refers to the distinctions in the number and types of exclusively Bodhisattvas versus a mixed Saṃgha of both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
The variety of the lands refers to the distinctions between those that are exclusively pure and those that are defiled or mixed.
The "variousness of sentient beings" refers to the distinctions such as those characterized by the admixture of greed, hatred, and delusion.
The "variousness of vehicles" refers to the distinctions such as the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.

What is called a "fault" refers to the questions posed by non-Buddhists and others regarding the arising of phenomena and the cessation of phenomena, the possible and the impossible; questions based on views of arising phenomena, questions based on views of ceasing phenomena, and questions based on views of defiled phenomena or pure phenomena—all such questions are defiled inquiries, and for this reason they are called faults.
When śrāvakas ask such questions as these—seeking cessation, seeking purity, or seeking the attainment of nirvāṇa—they do not attain great bodhi; therefore, this is called "transgression."

Even a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (bodhicitta) asks questions without correct mindfulness; because they have not yet perfected the pure wisdom that accords with reality, this is called a fault.
As for "benefit," if one does not ask in such a manner, it is called benefit; this meaning should be understood.
Questions such as these are "not correct questions" and so forth; questions such as these are called "correct questions" and so forth—this demonstrates their meaning.
As for what is called "arising," it refers to that which is neither a non-correct question nor a correct question—this demonstrates its meaning.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!
All dharmas are correct; all dharmas are erroneous.
What is the meaning of this?
The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all subsumed within the teachings of the Buddha.

Regarding the characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as previously explained, to say that the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is inconceivable as described is "correct," whereas to give rise to conceptual speculation regarding them is "erroneous. These constitute the matters of incorrect questioning and correct questioning.
As the sutra says: "Brahmā said:
'Jālinīprabha! For what reason?'"
Because all dharmas are inconceivable, all dharmas are called "correct.
If one conceives of that which is inconceivable, all dharmas are called "erroneous. Thus it is said.
For what reason are all phenomena inconceivable?
As the Sūtra states: "The tranquility of all phenomena is called right reflection."
Because it is free from the essence of false conceptualization, it is called "quiescent.
Because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is also called "quiescent.

Because they do not believe in the quiescence of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they fall into the extreme of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and cultivate various practices by falsely conceptualizing the objects of conceptualization. It is because they conceptualize the four great elements that they raise this question.

Regarding the statement that "the manifestation of the Dharma is not the correct inquiry into the true nature of the Dharma": to be free from one's own objective sphere and free from the limits of other desires is called the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena).
This is because it demonstrates the cause for the correct inquiry.
By what meaning is this intended?
By what kind of contemplation can one become free from desire?
And by what kind of wisdom does one know those phenomena?
The non-duality of those two is called *tathatā* (suchness). Within this, the characteristic of the wisdom of suchness—the non-conceptual wisdom—is called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*).
As for the term "limit of reality," it refers to the supreme limit that is free from all other desires.

What is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi) is that which is free from all desires; it refers to the characteristic of non-conceptualizing true suchness-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*). This is because, within the internal sphere of one's own objective realm, one observes the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) as they truly are.
In this sequence, it should be understood that clarity constitutes the quiescence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the "stages" (*bhūmi*): they consist in the accomplishment of the objective sphere of one's own mind and the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*).
Upon what phenomena do these stages of contemplation rest?
This refers to the phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) as they have been described.
Those aggregates and other phenomena are separated from *tathatā* (suchness), because that *tathatā* is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

One contemplates that *tathatā* through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and that wisdom is quiescent, because that *tathatā* is free from the sphere of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).
Thus he spoke this profound Dharma, knowing that this True Dharma is profound and difficult to understand.
As the *Jālinīprabha-bodhisattva* said:
"O Brahmā!..."
"Because there are few sentient beings who can understand the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in this way.

As it is said here regarding the true nature of all phenomena, one who seeks wisdom apart from the true nature of phenomena cannot find it; for that dharmatā transcends worldly categories of identity and difference.
Regarding the statement that "the substance of an existent phenomenon is not 'little,'" this is because it is based on the number one.
Apart from that number one, there is no further "small portion.

Thus, in order to negate the apprehension of a substantial entity, it is not that the substance of that phenomenon is absolutely non-existent; rather, it is because [the mind] does not perceive or know [it] that it negates the characteristic of non-existence.
What is the meaning of this statement?

Herein, it means that one has faith in the fact that the fundamental nature of all phenomena throughout the three periods of time is not perceived as having any objective characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*);

it does not mean that there is an actual realization of a negation. Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others do indeed possess the actual realization of the Dharma, yet they manifest this meaning; because they act in accordance with this meaning, it is called "faith" rather than "realization."
"One who realizes this Dharma is said to not see a single thing. Mañjushrī!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having heard such the true nature of all dharmas, practice with diligent effort, they are said to be practicing according to reality. This refers to the characteristics of those dharmas as explained within the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection.
As previously stated, one should understand this meaning: by relying on which mind and with which intention the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma.
Because he does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena, it is called the "Dharma of realization."
Because they know things as they truly are, such persons abide neither in the world nor in nirvāṇa.
Since not a single dharma is abandoned within the defilements of that world, there is no decrease.
Because not a single dharma is grasped within nirvāṇa, it does not increase;
this is shown to manifest that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not abide in the characteristics of either the mundane world or nirvāṇa.

Regarding those who hear the characteristics of the teaching of the True Dharma in this way: they first hear the Dharma from others, and subsequently engage in correct internal reflection; thus, they are able to successively give rise to supramundane right view and attain its fruit. This is because they demonstrate the reality-body by being free from all marks and not abiding in marks, and because they demonstrate non-abiding in nirvana as its cause.

This is because the Tathāgata perceives all phenomena as having the single flavor of selflessness; thus, he manifests that for all bodhisattvas, there is no discrimination between the faults of the world and the merits of nirvāṇa, as they possess the characteristic of equality. In this way, these bodhisattvas attain non-abiding in the world and non-abiding in nirvāṇa.
The sequential exposition of the Dharma has now reached its conclusion.
Furthermore, based on another meaning:
what is the significance clarified by the following inquiry?

When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he cannot transcend it; he cannot transcend the body; nor can he transcend the world to find yet another dharma. Therefore, there is not a single dharma diminished in the world, nor is there a single dharma increased within nirvāṇa, because he merely precludes the departure from one thing and precludes the acquisition of another.
By what meaning is this intended?
It does not mean that one who has not transcended the world is never able to transcend it; rather, it is for the purpose of refuting the view that [the world] is non-existent.
What meaning does this demonstrate?
This is because it manifests as being beyond two characteristics.
What is the meaning of this?
The "two characteristics" are: first, worldly activity; [and second, supramundane activity].
Second is nirvana.
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately abandoned both types of faults—the fault of conceptualizing the world and the fault of conceptualizing merit.
What is the meaning of this?
Within the dharma of equality, there is neither defilement nor purity; it is spoken thus because one relies upon the *dharmatā* of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) that is free from desire.

Since that reality-limit is fundamentally different from the world of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) due to its permanence, there is no one who enters *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, it is neither defiled nor pure.
In this sequence, it is not necessarily required to preach the Dharma; one may also dwell in silence while practicing all dharmas in accordance with the Dharma.
If one wishes to speak, one should do so as that Brahmā spoke; therefore, he was praised, saying, "Excellent, excellent!"
"The Dharma is ineffable, yet it can be spoken"—therefore, when the Tathāgata repeatedly praises, saying, "Excellent!
I do not apprehend birth-and-death, nor do I apprehend nirvāṇa," and so forth, he is first stating the meaning of what has been taught: that there is no further dharma whatsoever that can be spoken.
For what reason did the Tathāgata repeat this teaching?
Because five hundred bhikṣus became terrified upon hearing this teaching, the Tathāgata wished to bring those bhikṣus to ultimate certainty regarding this meaning.
What does this demonstrate?
It demonstrates that the intention of the Tathāgata is likewise so, not only that of Brahmā.

Sentient beings fall into the extreme of non-existence; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of emptiness in accordance with Brahmā. Those who practice the Brahma-conduct do not understand the profound meaning and engage in false conceptualization.
What is the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
It refers to the upholding of the precepts, practicing according to the teachings without transgression.
"Practicing the right path" means practicing the differentiated contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
The "dhyānas" refer to the four dhyānas, beginning with the first.
"Samādhis" refer to various modes of practice, such as those with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
"Samāpattis" refer to the four concentrations of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhyāna*).

Because those bhikṣus perceived the existence of phenomena and perceived the non-existence of phenomena, upon hearing the above teaching, they thought that the Tathāgata was asserting that there is absolutely nothing and that there is no practice of the holy life; therefore, they were struck with fear.

Because that bhikṣu perceives the existence of phenomena and perceives the non-existence of phenomena, in order to sever such views of existence and non-existence, it is said that for such a person, "the Buddha does not appear in the world" and so forth; this is because that person regards even nirvāṇa as a substantial entity and seeks to attain it, and [this teaching] serves as the antidote to this view of substantiality.
As it says in the Sūtra: "That person even seeks a definitive characteristic.
Having thus expounded the Dharma correctly based on the absence of names and marks, two parables are provided to rebuke those monks who were startled and terrified.
These two metaphors give rise to two causes for reflection: namely, the cause for generating the thought of revulsion and the cause for generating the thought of contemplation.
Because one attains nirvana by means of those two causes, they are thus censured.
What is the meaning demonstrated here?

It demonstrates that because one perceives the affliction of the mind through seeking the Dharma based on those [faults], one gives rise to the contemplation of revulsion; the first metaphor illustrates the remedial method through a corresponding similarity.

Because it manifests the contemplation of benefit, there arises the contemplation of joy due to the transformation of the body shared with others; this is the second simile, which corresponds to the remedial method.

Next, it clarifies that although such a person practices the correct characteristics, they are actually practicing erroneous characteristics, because they give rise to the characteristic of arising, give rise to the characteristic of cessation, perceive the characteristic of attaining nirvāṇa, and perceive the characteristic of realizing the Path.
The teachings previously expounded were heard by the bhikṣus, whereby their unwholesome conduct was slightly diminished;

from this point onward, however, they are intended to cause the bhikṣus to enter into the Dharma. Therefore, when the noble Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha requested the Brahmā to lead others into the Dharma, two aspects of the Dharma are manifested herein: first, the manifestation of the essential nature;
[second, the manifestation of the functional activity].
Second is the manifestation of attaining the fruit.
The term "substantial reality" is used to inspire faith in the Dharma.
The term "fruit" is used to enable one to abandon false views and attain liberation.

Because he ultimately manifests the characteristics of right view, he assumes the body of a bhikṣu to preach this Dharma here, thereby enabling the production of seeds; the Buddhas and Tathāgatas in other Buddha-lands likewise preach this same Dharma.
It clarifies that because those bhikṣus fear certain places yet have nowhere to go, they are unable to distance themselves from the characteristics of the dharmas being taught.

Since one cannot escape the fact that all places are not separate from dharmas and that [dharmas] are unavoidable, this characteristic is shown in such a way so that they do not depart; therefore, empty space is used as a metaphor.
To demonstrate this meaning:
where could one go to abandon fear? One never departs from the very place of which one is afraid.

Just as one who fears space cannot find a place—whether within space, beyond space, or devoid of space—to escape it, so too does one rely on that realized Dharma to manifest the attainment of its signs.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness should be understood as suchness.
Those who seek nirvāṇa and practice within the sphere of nirvāṇa yet do not attain it, do so because nirvāṇa is the pure characteristic of suchness.
By what meaning is this so?
Because that suchness is entirely equal within all phenomena, it is called nirvāṇa; for the verbal expressions used therein cannot be grasped.
What is the meaning of this?
It is to preclude the apprehension of those entities as substantial realities.

Thus, by remaining free from the extremes of existence and non-existence regarding things and phenomena, one is able to know the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.

When those bhikṣus had seen this, their minds attained liberation; having attained liberation of mind, they realized the true Dharma; and having realized the true Dharma, they themselves proclaimed the characteristics of dharmas.
Those bhikṣus were first ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), then became learners (*śaikṣa*), and finally attained arhatship.
For this reason, after these three stages, relying on their prior non-attainment, they spoke these words: "World-Honored One!..."
"We are now neither ordinary worldlings, nor those in training (śaikṣa), nor those beyond training (aśaikṣa), nor Arhats.
To "not abide in the world" means that within the realm of nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu), one has forever severed all bases for rebirth.

Regarding those who do not abide in *nirvāṇa*: because the grasping at the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) has not yet been exhausted within *nirvāṇa with remainder*, they manifest the appearance of a Buddha’s emergence in the world and the appearance of manifest realization and knowledge, as they truly are.
What is called "movement" is the distracted mind.
What is called the "notion of self" refers to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
What is called "arising" refers to the mental state capable of initiating volitional activity (*saṃskāra*).
What is called "play" (*krīḍā*) refers to the discriminating mind of the three phrases beginning with "movement.
Thus, whether cause or effect, he manifests that person as having a Buddha appear in the world.
Based on the Path, based on attainment, based on cessation, and based on realization, the noble Śāriputra questioned the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus should have answered in this manner.
As Śāriputra has said, the bhikṣus speak thus:
"I have attained the seven things that cannot be done, yet I engage in verbal discourse and questions and answers."
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the actual response and the counter-response.
This is of two kinds: first, the response by way of realization; [second, the response by way of refutation].
Second is the "answering by way of explanation.

Because such established responses exist, fellow bhikṣus who practice together find that their own preaching of the Dharma cannot reach the same depth; they develop a profound sense of respect, for they feel reverence toward that bhikṣu’s exposition of the essence of the Dharma.
The Commentary on the *Suvikrāntavikramīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
The Commentary on the *Suvikrāntavikramīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei Dynasty:

"Abiding in the field of merit, one is able to consume offerings" means that by abiding in the ground of the field of merit, one dwells in the path of the Arhat and is thus capable of receiving offerings.
Even the Great Master, the World-Honored One, was unable to digest all such offerings; how much less could we possibly digest them? What does this clarify?
It clarifies that one knows, according to reality, that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally pure.
For this reason, it is said: "Even the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, cannot fully digest such offerings, how much less can we?
What is the meaning of this?
It is because apart from the *dharmadhātu*, there is no one who receives offerings; for that *dharmadhātu* is primordially pure.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because those who abide on the ground of the field of merit abide on the ground of the Arhat and are worthy of receiving offerings, for they know the pure dharma-realm as it truly is.
Because the people of the world do not know that the Tathāgata is the supreme field of merit, it is said: "Even the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, cannot fully digest these offerings."
What is the meaning of this?

It is because apart from the *dharmadhātu*, there are no other distinct phenomena that are pure; for that *dharmadhātu* is pure by its very nature (*svabhāva*), it is the basis for receiving offerings, and it is the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) when questioned.
Next, one asks who those persons worthy of receiving offerings—the field of merit—are:
as the sutra subsequently states, "those who are not led astray by worldly dharmas."

The World-Honored One has thus explained, based on the fact that bodhisattvas are the field of merit for the world, the characteristics of the field of merit that receives offerings; therefore, he replied, "They are not led away by worldly dharmas."
What is the meaning of this?

It is because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others always dwell in the world and practice worldly dharmas, yet they are not defiled by worldly dharmas; although there are the various gates of worldly dharmas—such as victory and defeat, gain and loss, defamation and praise, and suffering and pleasure—they cannot lead them astray.
The essence of the bodhisattva’s mind is firm and steadfast; it does not follow these eight worldly dharmas.
With such a mind, it remains immovable and cannot be led astray by desire, hatred, or delusion.
Such a person is one who is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) worthy of receiving offerings.
This is called being a field of merit capable of receiving offerings; this constitutes purity.
For this reason, because of such a person who is a field of merit, the characteristics of a pure field of merit are inquired about.

Although bodhisattvas receive many followers, offerings, and gains, they do not give rise to the thought of grasping at even a single dharma or becoming attached to even a single dharma. For this reason, they are able to digest such offerings; as supreme fields of merit, they are able to digest offerings.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about being able to digest offerings.

"One who has no grasping or attachment" demonstrates the superior characteristics of one capable of receiving the field of merit; therefore, such a person attains the name of a field of merit possessing those two types of qualities.

Because bodhisattvas give rise to the bodhicitta so that sentient beings do not lose their peace and security, and because they cultivate those various merits for the sake of sentient beings, they attain those merits and become the most excellent among fields of merit worthy of offerings and respect.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about the pure field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Because they do not abandon the bodhicitta, they are pure fields of merit capable of receiving offerings.
Because these bodhisattvas are able to serve as fields of merit, gathering in sentient beings and acting as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), this meaning is demonstrated;
therefore, the question concerning the spiritual friend follows in sequence.

Practicing with a straightforward mind, they enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) through such a sequence; arising from that concentration, they bestow the bliss of peace and security upon all sentient beings. Because they do not abandon any sentient being, they manifest as the supreme and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of bodhisattvas.

In this way, the bodhisattva is able to act as a virtuous friend; relying on the teachings of the Tathāgata, they practice various deeds for their own benefit and the benefit of others, never failing in their gratitude toward the Teacher.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks how one can repay the Buddha’s kindness.

In order to attain bodhi and not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, and with a mind intent on benefiting others, one performs the supreme act of repaying the Buddha’s kindness regarding what He has done for oneself.
For one who repays this kindness, there are various meritorious practices such as making offerings and so forth.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about making offerings to the Buddha.

Since the Dharma-body, as the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), is by its very nature unarisen, one who can know that non-arising within the Tathāgata’s body realizes the mark of the ultimate reality. To seek that Dharma so as to surely attain it without loss, one should at all times make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva honors all Buddhas with supreme offerings.
Because he honors all Tathāgatas in this way, he draws near to them.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about drawing near to the Buddha.
This means that bodhisattvas would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than ever abandon the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Because they seek to embrace the practices of the ten stages, they do not forsake the prohibitive precepts and thereby attain a body in accordance with the Dharma; they draw near to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, manifesting superior conduct.
Because they have drawn near to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they give rise to a mind of respect and revere the Tathāgata; to demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about reverence for the Buddha.
By means of all sense faculties without distinction, one practices all forms of conduct for the sake of all faculties; therefore, no mind of affliction arises.
Because one is able to practice the thorough guarding of the sense faculties, one attains that esteemed and superior mind.
Having thus practiced correctly, the Bodhisattva attains great fruition.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next inquires about wealth.

By attaining the seven supreme spiritual riches, such as faith and the rest, which transcend the world, he demonstrates the mental state of the most excellent desire for these superior riches of the sublime Dharma.

Having already attained the severance of obstacles to practice and the abandonment of all marks of desire, one experiences the bliss of the Dharma and the bliss of food and drink, and realizes the Dharma as it truly is.

One practices in accordance with reality through faith, ethical discipline, shame, dread of blame, learning, generosity, and wisdom; the giving of material wealth is explained according to its proper sequence.
Furthermore, regarding the two kinds of dharma-wealth, shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*), one should understand them as the methods for severing the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although a bodhisattva possesses these seven kinds of dharma-wealth, they do not give rise to the thought, "Is my store sufficient or insufficient?"
To demonstrate this meaning, he asks in succession about contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*).

For the sake of gathering in all sentient beings, although a bodhisattva seeks offerings and respect, his mind always seeks unsurpassed *prajñā*; not considering these sufficient and not giving rise to a sense of having attained enough is called contentment.
Having attained contentment, one becomes detached from all desires.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about seclusion (*viveka*).
Although a bodhisattva moves within the three realms, he does not seek those places, because he has attained the supreme mind of tranquility.
Having attained this supreme, tranquil state of mind, he is detached from both body and mind; it is to demonstrate this meaning that he next asks about the absence of unwholesome conduct.
Although the Bodhisattva enjoys various excellent and sublime sensory objects, his mind is not defiled by afflictions, because he has attained this superior mind and guards his sense faculties.
Once the Bodhisattva has attained the guarding of the sense faculties, he is free from fear in all circumstances; because he is without fear, he attains peace and happiness.
To demonstrate this meaning, he asks the person who is happy in successive order.

Although the bodhisattva receives offerings and respect, he does not become greedily attached to them; he never abandons any sentient being, and by knowing all conditioned phenomena as they truly are and remaining free from all afflictions, he attains supreme bliss.

Thus, having attained supreme bliss by being unattached and free from all afflictions, one does not abandon sentient beings who experience suffering; in this way, one is able to reach the other shore.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about "being able to reach the other shore.

Because Bodhisattvas manifest bodies with the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) within the various realms of existence (*gati*) to gather in all sentient beings who possess the six sense bases—thereby severing their desires and causing them to attain the other shore through a mind free from craving—they are said to be "able to relinquish the six sense bases."
By relinquishing the six sense bases, one attains the superior mind that reaches the further shore.
Because the Bodhisattva thus attains the superior mind and reaches the further shore, they abide correctly in that state.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks about abiding on the other shore.

By means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which does not differentiate between the paths of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, one realizes the dharma of selflessness, abides in non-abiding nirvāṇa, and attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
For this reason, in the eighth stage, one attains the wisdom of both sameness and difference; therefore, it is called "reaching the other shore and abiding in the supreme place.
When a bodhisattva thus abides on the other shore, they fulfill the supramundane pāramitās.
To demonstrate this meaning, he next asks: "How are the various pāramitās increased?
Because one seeks the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), giving and the other perfections increase;
and because giving and the others increase through mutual reinforcement, the bodhisattva teaches the mind of omniscience to all sentient beings.

In order to cause sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta and increase their practice of giving, Bodhisattvas have, in previous lives, already caused those sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta and practice generosity.

In this way, the bodhisattvas themselves practice giving and teach others to practice giving; furthermore, they transform and guide other sentient beings to practice giving. Those bodhisattvas also cause sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta and practice giving, and those bodhisattvas further cause sentient beings to resolve their minds and practice giving.
In this way, by successively establishing one's own mind in giving and causing others to abide in giving,
the perfection of giving increases through this reciprocal process, because one never abandons the bodhicitta.
He teaches the perfection of ethical discipline so that others who have violated their vows may attain it.

He teaches the perfection of patience because he does not abandon the mind of bodhisattva conduct, for the sake of attaining great enlightenment, for the sake of establishing others in ethical discipline, and because he perceives that his mind directed toward omniscience never regresses.
The name "Bodhisattva" is spoken within the context of the bodhicitta in order to cause other beings in other places to give rise to a mind of patience.
Because one endures all offenses and endures all evils, yet finds that the mind of omniscience cannot be attained through such means, the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) is taught.
Relying on the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), one does not perceive a "far shore" nor grasp at the characteristics of ascetic practices; therefore, no mind of weariness arises.

Because one realizes that the mind of omniscience is quiescent, the Dharma of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is taught—namely, that the intrinsic nature of the mind is pure, unborn, and undying. Because of knowing this wisdom of quiescence, because the distracted mind does not function at all, and because one does not conceptualize any phenomena, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is taught.
Because it encompasses non-conceptual wisdom, and because it manifests the complete purification of the other perfections, it is taught that the other perfections depend upon the mind of omniscience.

Regarding the remedial dharmas for the afflictions that obstruct practice: it is solely through such superior practice of the perfection of vision (*darśana-pāramitā*) regarding non-self that the Buddha-dharma is brought to maturity and sentient beings are transformed; thus, based upon those dharmas, one subsequently asks about the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
One does not give rise to the notion of "self" toward sentient beings, but rather gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
What does this clarify?
It means that because there is no mind seeking security for anything other than one's own self, one does not conceive of other sentient beings as being distinct from oneself.

The Bodhisattva practices compassion based on that perception of the non-arising of phenomena; because he perceives that the phenomena of suffering are not established, and because sentient beings are attached to the suffering of suffering, he gives rise to a compassionate mind.

Relying upon that, the bodhisattva does not give rise to the notion of a self while practicing sympathetic joy (*muditā*); relying upon that, they perceive their own body as being detached from sympathetic joy.
When seeing others' means of subsistence fully accomplished, they do not give rise to a mind of greed or envy, nor does sympathetic joy fail to arise.

The bodhisattva is not like this; being free from any further signs of greed, they rejoice in those [others]. Therefore, having distanced themselves from the discordant factor of envy (*īrṣyā*), they rely on the absence of envy to practice sympathetic joy.
The bodhisattva relies upon that [insight] and, not giving rise to the notions of "self" and "other," practices equanimity.
Relying on the vision of the notions of "self" and "other," he practices equanimity as an antidote thereto.

In the eighth stage, there is effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), because one has attained the power of non-conceptualizing wisdom, because one has attained the power of wisdom that is both identical and non-identical, because one is able to remain far removed from the characteristics of the two minds of self and other, and because one provides sentient beings with the skillful means for the cause of detachment from defilement.

Thus, for one who practices based on the perfections and the immeasurables for the sake of benefiting both oneself and others, there is furthermore reliance upon ever-increasing aspiration, reliance upon the experience of the joy of the Dharma, and reliance upon the abandonment of afflictions, so that all the aforementioned virtues may increase.
Next, it is asked: how does one abide in faith and so forth?
Following that sequence, one is able to believe in the ineffable Dharma and thus abides in the Dharma of faith.

Having believed in the foremost Dharma—the profound Dharma of non-self—one gains faith in other profound Dharmas that are otherwise difficult to believe. By not clinging to any sounds, one abides within the wisdom of hearing; regarding the Dharma as heard, there is no such mind of attachment nor any seeking of the Dharma elsewhere. Although one’s wisdom of hearing may be slight, one is able to accomplish much because merely hearing a single verse of practice constitutes great wisdom through extensive learning.

Based on internal mental characteristics, there is a sense of shame (*hrī*); that is to say, by relying on the conduct of others and oneself that is contrary to the Dharma, one recognizes the fault and distances oneself from it, thereby abandoning external objects and accomplishing the practice of moral dread (*apatrāpya*).
When others teach the Dharma but do not practice it according to the Dharma, one abandons those faults because the person of another is an external sense-base (*bāhyāyatana*).
When envy enters and one speaks of that person in such a way, abandoning that teaching is called "abandoning the external sense-base."
This meaning should be understood:

the three types of action—of body, speech, and mind—are pure; they accomplish merit in all circumstances and are worthy of receiving offerings. From the purity of the field of merit and so forth, up to a sense of shame and dread of blame, these aforementioned virtues serve as antidotes to their respective opposites—the unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind. For this reason, they are called "pure."
Because he is endowed with the merit of reaching that [state], he is therefore called "the one who traverses all places of merit"; this is how it should be understood.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
"pervading all places of merit" means dwelling within all those aforementioned dharmas of merit.
The meaning of these ten verses corresponds exactly to the Sūtra.

Having thus explained, according to worldly conventions, the various merits such as being a supreme field of merit capable of receiving offerings, one should understand that the Brahmā subsequently poses questions based on those very meanings in this sequential order.

What is meant by a bodhisattva transcending worldly dharmas? Since the śrāvakas also transcend the world, the Tathāgata manifests a superior dharma that surpasses the supramundane dharmas of the śrāvakas; therefore, it is said that he transcends worldly dharmas.

Furthermore, he manifests that although he dwells in the world and practices worldly dharmas, he transcends the world; yet he is not defiled or attached by those worldly dharmas, because he manifests the practice of worldly ways in order to transform sentient beings.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Because he knows all worldly phenomena as they truly are.
Furthermore, for the sake of gathering all sentient beings, he manifests skillful means for those beings to attract them and cause them to enter into worldly phenomena.

Knowing the truth of the origin of the world and knowing the destination of the world, one is born in those places by relying on the wisdom of aspiration, because one is not produced by the origin of the world.

Taking birth in such a manner, he manifests in the world to accomplish conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); relying upon conventional truth, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may transcend the world.
Although a bodhisattva acts within the world, they are ultimately never defiled by the world.

Having attained the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and abiding in the path of non-abiding, they act for the sake of teaching and transforming all sentient beings; therefore, although they are born into the world, it is for the purpose of embracing the way of the world.
The thirty-five verses are as explained in the Sūtra.

Relying on the exposition of worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*), the Tathāgata likewise relies upon his own cognition of the world of persons and the world of phenomena (*dharma-loka*) as objects of knowledge, and through the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), he explains the entry into the characteristics of worldly phenomena.

Because the Dharma of the Tathāgata transcends the supramundane dharmas of the śrāvakas, and while the śrāvakas also transcend the mundane sphere, the Tathāgata transcends even those spheres of the śrāvakas and further teaches the superior Dharma.
Regarding the statement, "The one who teaches that Dharma, for the sake of other sentient beings transcending the world, manifests such supramundane skillful means," and the words,
"Brahmā said: 'As for the world,

I say the five aggregates are called the world,'" it should be understood that this demonstrates the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), because it is spoken in reference to the mundane world.
To be greedily attached to the five aggregates is to be greedily attached to this craving.
It is called the "origination of the world" because, by depending on that craving, the world is accumulated.

Because the aggregates (*skandha*) of the past, future, and present have ceased, and because the causes for the aggregates of the future life have been exhausted and no further seeds for the future have been sown, they are called "ceased."

Regarding the observation of the five aggregates such that one does not perceive duality, which is called the path to the cessation of the world: seeking the path and not seeking the path are one and the same.
Duality never attains the noble path; this is shown for the sake of manifesting excellence.
What does this clarify?
The worldly antidote is not invariably fixed: if there is an antidote, one is able to become weary of suffering; if there is no antidote, one regresses from that state.
If a single phenomenon serves as an antidote to a particular phenomenon, it does not serve as an antidote to other phenomena.
If there were a single dharma that served as an antidote for a lower stage, it would not be an antidote for a higher stage;
however, the noble path is not like this, because it serves as an antidote for all dharmas at all times.

Having thus explained the distinctions of the worldly and other [categories] according to the meaning of the remedies of the Śrāvaka-yāna, next, the distinctions of the meaning of the remedial dharmas according to the Mahāyāna are explained.
Regarding those who teach the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) based on the Mahāyāna, it is as the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, Brahmā!

For these reasons, that which is called the 'five aggregates' is merely a verbal expression. This is because within the five aggregates, seeing, hearing, knowing, and so forth, are merely names explained through conceptual differentiation.
Because it relies on what has been accumulated over beginningless eons and relies on the essence of conceptualization, one becomes attached to those phenomena.
The Bodhisattva observes that if one relies on such conceptualization of names, this is the world of linguistic views;
if one greedily clings to the signs of conceptualization according to words and names, that constitutes wrong view and a departure from compliant practice, which is called the "arising of the world."

Just as there is the characteristic of cessation in that world, one observes the essence of the characteristic of cessation as it truly is; because one observes the cessation of the object of focus as it truly is, it is called the cessation of the world.
By what path does one not grasp those views, such that it is called the "worldly path of cessation"?
As previously stated, the analysis that can counteract analysis demonstrates non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The Tathāgata has already transcended such worldly realms; because the Tathāgata has attained Great Nirvāṇa, he has embraced the path that neither transcends the world nor is it apart from the world.

Having thus explained the Truth of Suffering and the others by way of the mundane and the mundane-like, [the text] next asks again regarding the Four Noble Truths taught by the Tathāgata: while those noble ones conceptually differentiate the various truths such as suffering through false discrimination, the Tathāgata reveals the true Noble Truths in a manner that is not like this.
By what meaning is this so?
There are two kinds of truths: first, the truth of characteristics (lakṣaṇatattva); [second, the truth of ultimate reality].
Second is the truth of mind (*cittatattva*).
Because one relies upon these two kinds of truths:

regarding the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*), it refers to all the characteristics of phenomena, the essence of phenomena, and the substantial reality of phenomena such as the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); because there is no distinction between those non-noble truths and the noble truths, it is called the noble truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
Regarding the truth based on the mind, it refers to the supreme noble truths; for within those noble truths, one knows the inverted mind and the non-inverted mind.
What is the meaning of this?
When those who are not noble ones speak of the Truth of Suffering, they merely experience suffering and do not know the Truth of Suffering;
when they speak of the Truth of Origination, they merely hear of false and illusory causes of origination and do not know the Truth of Origination;
when they speak of the Truth of Cessation, they hear the name "cessation" and fall into the view of nihilism, not knowing the Truth of Cessation.

Regarding the Truth of the Path, such a person merely hears of karma and afflictions as conditioned phenomena; since such phenomena are merely the conditioned, worldly dharma of origination, they do not know the Truth of the Path.
In this way, one discriminates the four truths, beginning with the truth of suffering.

If all such things were truths, then all sentient beings born in the three evil realms would likewise possess truths; yet they do not possess them. It is for the purpose of manifesting this meaning that the Sūtra says: "Brahmā!..."
If that suffering were a truly real noble truth, then all cattle, pigs, and other animals should also possess a truly real truth.
Why is this? Because they all likewise undergo various forms of suffering.
For this reason, suffering is not a true reality (*satya*), and so forth.

For what reason are only oxen and pigs mentioned among the animals and no others? It is because among animals, only oxen and pigs are the most ignorant; it is because all people in the world know that oxen and pigs are the most dull-witted.
In this way, one should understand that what is non-noble and falsely discriminated is taken to be the truth:
worldly people, relying on the door of suffering, falsely cling to it as the Truth of Suffering;
relying on the door of origination, they falsely cling to it as the Truth of Origination.
Relying on the gate of cessation (*nirodha-mukha*), they falsely cling to the desire to be free from contaminated phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*) as the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*);
relying on the gate of the antidote of the Path (*mārga-pratipakṣa-mukha*), they falsely cling to it as the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

Furthermore, the two truths of suffering and its origin lack that essential nature and characteristic, because their own essence is not established, and because their own essence is fundamentally unarisen and non-composite.
Because it serves as the antidote to that mind of false attachment, it is taught that one knows there is no arising and no combination; this is called the Noble Truth of the Sages.
Furthermore, all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) likewise lack such a substantial nature at all times, because the essence of those phenomena is inherently inseparable [from emptiness].

Because it relies on the antidote to that mind of false attachment, and because all those phenomena are primordially quiescent by virtue of the purity of *tathatā*, one speaks of knowing them as neither arising nor ceasing; this is called the noble ones’ antidote to the noble truths.
The antidote likewise lacks that essential nature and characteristic, because its own substance is not established, and because that Truth of the Path is not itself an antidotal truth.

It is by means of the antidote to the mind of false attachment, by relying on the naturally pure mind, by relying on the contemplation of equality, by relying on the wisdom of maturity, by relying on the wisdom of discernment, and by relying on the equality and non-duality of all phenomena—that one attains the Path through the non-dual Dharma. This is called the Noble Truth of the Sages.
Because it is taught as a synonym for Nirvana, the foremost noble truth, it is called the Truth of the Path; this is what is known as the noble truth of the noble ones.
It is called a noble truth because it is non-deceptive and because it is unarisen.

Furthermore, from non-arising up to non-duality—meaning that because all phenomena are equal by virtue of relying on the path cultivated in accordance with nirvāṇa and relying on the noble truth of the path—all phenomena are said to be non-dual.

That which is called "nirvāṇa" is designated by the name based on the purity of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness); for that nirvāṇa is free from the dharmas of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), and it is named in dependence upon that dharma.
In this successive order, furthermore,
that which is called "truth" when based on improper mindfulness is termed false speech and is not the actual Noble Truth.
Moreover, that same truth, when based on proper mindfulness, is termed true speech, yet it too is not the actual Noble Truth.
Therefore, it is demonstrated that both false speech and true speech are ultimately unestablished.
As the Sūtra says: "Brahmā!
Regarding 'the true noble truth, the true noble truth,' it is because it is neither false speech nor true speech."
It should be understood that they manifest as if grasping at the characteristics of a self through incorrect mindfulness.
It should be understood that because one gives rise to attachment toward each and every phenomenon through such phrases, one is bound by the characteristics of various and distinct meanings.

It is said that there is a self, taking the existence of the self-essence as the fundamental basis; because various phenomena exist in dependence upon this fundamental self, [the following designations arise]:

because the self is uninterrupted, it is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*); because it dwells in dependence on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), it is called "life"; and because it repeatedly falls into the six realms of existence, it is called a "person" (*puruṣa*).

Thus, seeing oneself as a single entity and falsely clinging to the characteristics of a self, one engages in false conceptualization regarding that self as either permanent or impermanent, thereby falling into the view of eternalism or the view of nihilism.
To perceive "this is my form" and "I am formless," and so forth—these various false discriminations and diverse attachments result in clinging to a singular self.

Because one regards the self as a substantial entity, one grasps at signs through such false discrimination; relying on that false discrimination of a self, one grasps at ignorance and other factors, giving rise to false discrimination and thereby grasping at the characteristic of birth.
Thus, based on that, one falsely discriminates the cessation of ignorance and so forth, grasping at the characteristic of annihilation.
Such arising and ceasing depend upon the mark of a self.
In succession, one accomplishes that false discrimination, grasping at the signs of the world and grasping at the signs of nirvāṇa.

To grasp at that world and to grasp at nirvāṇa refers to the various modes of grasping at signs as previously explained; that which is called "grasping" consists of the firm attachment and definitive apprehension of false discriminations such as longing, desire, and faith.
To hold that "only this is real and all else is false" is called attachment.
Because those various views cannot be relinquished, such false clinging is called contact (*sparśa*).
Not being separated from that contact is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
Thus, in this sequence, not adhering, not contacting, and not clinging are called "true speech," which demonstrates right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

Having thus taught the Dharma based on the non-self of the person—which is neither false speech nor true speech—he next teaches the analysis of suffering and so forth based on the non-self of phenomena.

Because it is devoid of non-conceptual wisdom, it is called "deception"; because of this deception, it is termed "false speech. Therefore, he demonstrates that the truths of those two vehicles are illusory and unreal.
Because one discriminates all phenomena of the three periods of time, that mindfulness is false; therefore, non-discriminative wisdom is manifested.
What is the meaning of this?

It is because one recollects all dharma-gates of the past, discriminates all dharmas of the present, and recollects all dharma-gates of the future; for these reasons, one is detached from correct mindfulness.

Abiding in that non-conceptual wisdom, the bodhisattva does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding the characteristics of any phenomena; by contemplating the selflessness of phenomena, they attain the nirvana of non-abiding. Because they do not dwell in either samsara or nirvana, they attain the vision of equality.
When a bodhisattva has thus skillfully understood the dharmas, they manifest the truths as they have been taught, because they do not perceive the attainment of those truths.
Regarding the truths of the noble ones, there is neither true speech nor false speech therein; for this reason, they manifest that meaning.
Although there is a distinction between the two types of mind—right mindfulness and wrong mindfulness—the Noble Truths are still not realized.
If one dwells in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and realizes the Truths, then at all times, throughout past and present, one always and eternally abides in suchness.
From this point onward, the meaning of that is demonstrated.
As the Sūtra says: "O Brahmā!
That which is called 'real and real' is so because it has been real from antiquity."
What does this clarify?
That *dharmatā* and *dharmatattva* manifest as the cause for the supreme *dharmatattva* and the *ārya-dharmatattva*.
Because there is no distinction between the mundane world and *nirvāṇa*, it is therefore called the "eternal noble truth" (*nitya-āryasatya*).
Based on the two manifestations of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the two noble truths are established.

Thus, based on the noble truth of the characteristic of suchness, one manifests that the noble truth of saṃsāra is not to be abandoned, and one manifests that the noble truth of nirvāṇa is not to be grasped.
Thus, regarding one who speaks of the characteristics of the truths after having realized them, it is shown that such a person is called a speaker of truth;
yet, for that person, speaking of the noble truths [as they are conventionally perceived] would be called false speech.
From this point onward, the meaning is demonstrated.

It is shown that such a person lacks the cause for training in higher ethics; because they cannot guard the sense faculties, it is shown that due to this deficiency in causes, they lack training in higher ethics.
Furthermore, because they lack the cause for training in higher concentration, it is shown that they lack training in higher concentration.
Because there is no cause for that training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*), it is shown that there is no training in higher wisdom.

It is shown that these are signs of birth, the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and so forth—attachments to false phenomena—which are to be sequentially correlated with themselves; this meaning should be understood.
Thus, while that Blessed One is the World-Honored One, those śrāvakas are merely followers of external paths (tīrthikas).

Next, it is shown that those śrāvakas become externalists because those foolish people take the loss of things to be the truth and take the existence of things to be the truth; this demonstrates that such people fall into the evil realms.

Because I do not speak and because the Tathāgata has attained the dharma that is beyond speech, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the various truths, such as suffering, is not established; thus, I demonstrate and explain the characteristics of the truths.
In this way, I have realized them, manifesting the fact that no characteristic of an existing entity is established.
Because it manifests as that which others do not grasp, awakening (bodhi) is unattainable.

It is not grasped because its essence is non-conceptual; thus, one thinks, "I have attained the dharma of awakening," yet there is no such grasping. It is free from all existence, for it is detached from the three realms and the five destinies, and because it transcends those dharmas by attaining the supramundane dharma of the noble path.

Thus, not seeing any phenomena as having the characteristic of bodhi, and not realizing a single phenomenon while realizing all phenomena, for this reason he is called the One Who Should Be Fully Awakened to Truth (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
If the Tathāgata has no attainment regarding dharmas, for what reason is it said that the Tathāgata sitting at the site of enlightenment is called a Buddha?
This question is intended to refute the notion that there is a substantial entity to be attained.
The Tathāgata says, "I do not obtain any entity," because the name "Dharma" heard in teaching is subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
it is because of the characteristic of conceptual differentiation that, based on dharmas that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), he speaks of a "self."
Next, according to the teaching on the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one asks:
regarding those phenomena and that selflessness of phenomena, since all phenomena take non-substantiality as their essence, they exclude both the extremes of existence and non-existence.
What is the meaning of "manifestation"?

It means manifesting that those dharmas are not something existent that can be realized, nor are they something non-existent that can be realized; because those dharmas are free from these two characteristics, they are said to be "realized."
Having spoken thus, it is next explained that this does not mean one entirely fails to realize the true Dharma.

Because one perceives that dharmas do not exist through false attachment, one correctly understands that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is unarisen, arising instead based on the essence of others through inversion.
That which is called the essential nature of the conceptualization of defilement and so forth is eternally, at all times, unborn by its own nature;
one knows that suchness and the self are the Dharma thus realized. How is this known?
It is known as that which is known through non-knowing and non-perception, as is the case at all times.

To speak of "knowledge" is a manifestation intended to show that even the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*) is non-conceptual; for one does not perceive a real essence (*dharmakāya*) therein, since no verbal expression can be found regarding that essence. Therefore, this demonstrates the cause of that realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*).
Regarding the phrases "not knowing," "not recognizing," "not seeing," and so forth, these fall into four types of discourse concerning seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing.
It should be understood that these various phrases are presented as a progressive sequence of gates.
"Cannot be grasped by seeing, etc. means that just as the intrinsic nature of those phenomena is such, those phenomena cannot be grasped by means of seeing and so forth.
What is the meaning of this?

Because all names are unattainable; because it transcends the sphere of the mind; because it is free from the phenomena of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because it cannot be correlated within the realm of corresponding dharmas; because no speech can reach it; because it cannot be correlated within the realm of corresponding dharmas; because it cannot be questioned or answered; because it transcends the six sense faculties; because it transcends names; because nothing within the internal body can be expressed of it; because it lacks worldly characteristics; because worldly dharmas do not operate therein; because it is detached from activity as conditioned dharmas do not function there; because it lacks the characteristics of the worldly mind, mentation, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) that differentiate; because it has transcended the world as it lacks any substantial entity; and because, having transcended conceptual proliferation, there is no object with which it could be contrasted.
Having thus demonstrated that the essence of the taught Dharma is entirely free from all conceptual constructions, one should know that this Dharma is shown to be similar to space.
That the Dharma is similar to space should be understood through two aspects:

first, its universal pervasiveness, because it is free from the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of existence and non-existence, and because it attains the inconceivable, ultimate Dharma of all Buddhas.

Second is non-obstruction: because one is able to perform what could not otherwise be done through the supreme endurance of suffering with a mind of great compassion; because one relies upon verbal discourse to express the wordless Dharma; and because one causes all sentient beings to enter the Dharma by relying upon that teaching.
To demonstrate what meaning?

There are sentient beings who, relying on a mind of cleverness and self-conceit, are unable to believe in these explained characteristics of phenomena; this is shown because the roots of goodness of those sentient beings are meager.
In explaining the characteristics of those dharmas, what meaning is being clarified?
It clarifies that this dharma-gate is difficult for all the world to believe, because worldly minds are constantly inverted regarding things that are identical in nature.
What is the meaning of this?

People of the world think to themselves: "We should realize the true truths; by fulfilling our practice according to the Dharma of the three trainings, we shall, by relying on that Dharma, attain nirvana."
One-pointedly cultivating wholesome dharmas, one experiences the joy of the Dharma in the present by relying upon those dharmas.

This sequence of virtuous practice takes the appearance of a Buddha in the world as its foundation; next comes the teaching of the Dharma; and next, the Saṃgha of companions who practice according to reality. Thus, these dharmas abide in accordance with the true reality, for they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
One should understand that this meaning is something that people of the world cannot believe.
"World-Honored One!
It is as if fire were to emerge from water, or water were to emerge from fire"—what meaning does this demonstrate?
It is considered that afflictions are manifested as fire because they are not of a tranquil nature and one must distance oneself from that nature;
awakening is like water because it is able to extinguish the fire of afflictions.
One should understand this principle: that lack of faith and faith are mutually exclusive; they are associated [with different mental states] and do not coexist.
As for what is called "affliction," it refers to all ignorant ordinary beings who, through such attachment to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), claim that afflictions defile the self.

This is because the essence of afflictions is not established for those foolish people; because phenomena are observed to be unattainable; because they are realized through supramundane wisdom; because consciousness cannot analytically discern them; because one trains in the path by means of the antidote and that which is to be countered; because one does not cling to the dual characteristics of the antidote and the counteracted; because one attains the pure dharma of *tathatā*; because there is no mind that grasps or acquires phenomena; because it renders those obstacles powerless; and because the nature of those obstructive phenomena is fundamentally non-arising.

As for the teaching on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), if a person does not give rise to the characteristics of various phenomena, they will then be able to distance themselves from all false views and attain liberation; this is because by distancing themselves from grasping at unreal characteristics, they can eliminate the dualistic mind of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*) that is to be remedied and its remedy.
From this point onward, based on the merit of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas' faith in the Dharma, one should understand that the praise of those bodhisattvas concerns seven kinds of merit.
What are the seven?
First, the fulfillment of the merit of all performed practices;
second, the merit of cultivation;
Third, the merit of entering the stages;
fourth, the merit of generating existence through a mind of mastery;
fifth, the merit of skillful cultivation.
Sixth is the merit of being able to accumulate the qualities of practicing the Buddha-dharma;
seventh is the merit of attaining the fruit.
What is the merit of fulfilling all performed practices?
This is because he manifests that, regarding the Buddhas of the past, all the various merits to be performed and have been performed are already fully accomplished.
Furthermore, what is the meaning?
It is based on two kinds of meanings:
First, reliance on merit;
second, reliance on wisdom.
This is because they are able to provide offerings, respect, and service, and because their various practices and so forth accord with proper decorum, as well as because they hear the true Dharma.

When a bodhisattva has thus fulfilled the practices of merit and wisdom in this sequential order, they should next practice the various deeds for entering the stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, the fourfold verses on the cultivation of merit are explained next, demonstrating that there is a further increase in merit and wisdom through the two types of sustenance: physical food and the food of the Dharma.

By relying on spiritual friends and further cultivating all practices, one is able to exercise skillful means regarding both meaning and phenomena; because one practices in accordance with the true Dharma as it truly is, and by virtue of having attained the power of supreme and wondrous roots of goodness, as well as by relying on skillful means.
Excellence is of two kinds:
first, excellence in terms of the agent and the action;
second, profound excellence.

They are able to believe in that state because they hear these two kinds of great and wondrous teachings without being startled or terrified; because they skillfully protect the Tathāgata’s treasury of the sublime Dharma; because they practice in accordance with reality, following each teaching exactly as it was spoken; and because they do not perceive a self nor do they come into contact with phenomena.

When a bodhisattva practices in this manner according to reality, they ultimately enter the bodhisattva stage; therefore, twenty-five phrases concerning the merit of entering the stage are taught next to demonstrate this meaning.
What is meant by "being born into the family of the Tathāgata"?
It is because this bodhisattva is born into the family of the Buddha and attains the Buddha-dharma.

This is because they are able to abandon the afflictions of conceptual discrimination and at that time apprehend non-conceptual wisdom; because they manifest the practice of the perfections such as generosity; and because they have severed the dharma of breaking precepts, which is the object to be remedied.
What is the meaning of this?
Because of upholding the precepts, one stands in contrast to the breaking of them;
since the various afflictions that give rise to the breaking of precepts are thereby extinguished, upholding the precepts serves as the remedy for that which is to be remedied.

Because it serves as the antidote to cherishing one's body and life; because it serves as the antidote to the mind of indolence; because it serves as the antidote to the evil and unwholesome of the desire realm; and because it serves as the antidote to all incorrect views, even down to those of the Hīnayāna—it is thus called the merit of entering the stage.

One should know that these are the merits of the supramundane practice of the pāramitās, because they consist of the merit of correctly entering into the profound Dharma as truly taught by the Tathāgata, without inversion.

Because he cannot create obstacles to various meritorious virtues—namely, because celestial Māras, affliction-Māras, and so forth cannot create obstacles—the sequence is explained as follows: because he is able to enter into meritorious virtues by preaching the Dharma; because he enters into the merit of the non-erroneous Dharma through profound intention; and because the merit of preaching the Dharma consists of explaining according to reality both conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus it is explained in successive order.
What does this clarify? Regarding the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*), it should be understood as the entry into the intrinsic characteristics (*svabhāvalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
This is because one attains the pure dharma by entering the stage of the stream of the Dharma-gate (*dharmamukhasrotas*) which sustains meritorious qualities (*guṇadhāraṇa*).

Because they are able to perform what is to be done by relying on the power of the Tathāgata’s sustaining presence; because these bodhisattvas share the uncommon dwelling-merit of the same holy life (*brahmacarya*); because they have attained the equal practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*); because these bodhisattvas possess a portion of wholesome dharmas that increases their merit; and because supramundane merits such as faith and so forth are all manifest before them.
This refers to the merit of not partaking in various foods.
What does this clarify? It means obtaining food as circumstances allow.

This refers to the merit of contentment regarding alms-food, dwellings, bedding, medicinal requisites, and so forth; because it is practiced by the Noble Ones, one does not become attached to any means of subsistence whatsoever, and thus it is the characteristic of practice that delights in detachment from all desires.
One should understand that this is the opposite of contact with merit.
Furthermore, what is its meaning?
It means not depending on others for the sustenance of one's wisdom; therefore, one should understand that such a person is easy to satisfy and easy to support.
Because one can accord with the merit of realized wisdom and will ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* oneself, and because the mind is certain that "I shall surely attain it."

One should know that such a person is a "capable deliverer," because they are able to deliver those who have not yet been delivered; these eight phrases, beginning with this, constitute the merit of practicing for the benefit of others, and should be understood in this way.

Because they are able to comfort sentient beings bound by afflictions and cause them to enter the Path; because they are able to establish sentient beings within the Dharma of liberation; and because they are able to bring sentient beings to attain liberation—these two phrases sequentially demonstrate the superior state: being able to expound the Path and being able to grant liberation.

The two phrases sequentially demonstrate the ability to know the remedial dharmas; they demonstrate the ability to provide the remedies, as well as the relationship between the remedied and the remedial dharmas.
*Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
*Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Four.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei Dynasty:
Having thus entered the stage of a bodhisattva, because he gives rise to the mind that seeks to benefit all sentient beings, he gathers [them] into the various realms of existence.
