Therefore, it is next explained that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is born within the three realms of existence by means of a mind of mastery; for this reason, it is called the "fourfold demonstration of the manifestation of the acquisition of merit."
Because they take birth in superior realms through the power of mastery, and although they are born in those places, they are not defiled by them;
because they do not grow weary of taking up their place of birth over a vast period of time;
and because they do not arise through the power of others—such as afflictions or karma—but rather take birth according to their own sovereign will.
Because Bodhisattvas are born in all places and do not fear the various kinds of suffering and affliction experienced therein.

Thus, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, Bodhisattvas practice all manner of deeds and always serve as leaders among all sentient beings; therefore, it is said next that they can act as leaders, lead the great assembly, and accomplish meritorious virtues, with fifteen phrases demonstrating this meaning.

Because the Bodhisattva diligently studies the methods of practice as taught by the Buddha himself and instructs others without fault; and because he trains in the prohibitions and precepts over a long period of time, upholding them without violation, guarding them with vigilance, and maintaining them with firm resolve.
Because he is well-established in these two kinds of merit at both earlier and later times, for this reason he is able to lead the great assembly; this meaning should be understood.

It is because they can act as leaders for sentient beings to bring them under subdual; because these bodhisattvas are able to lead the great assembly and no māras can create obstacles or difficulties for them, as they have distanced themselves from all māra-activities;
because they possess the attainment of non-guarded conduct in body, speech, and mind, and thus do not fear others speaking of their faults;
and because, having directly perceived the profound Dharma, they are able to answer difficult questions without timidity due to their superior skillful means in preaching the Dharma.
Because he leads the great assembly to perform great deeds and cultivate all practices, he does not retreat from his own portion of roots of goodness.

These two phrases demonstrate that he causes those beings who can be transformed to be born into clarity; because he enables those beings who can be transformed to depart from ignorance, he acts as a causal condition. This sequence of meaning should be understood in this way.

Because among sentient beings there are those who are compliant and those who are non-compliant, his mind remains firm; for although there are afflictions that are contradictory and those that are not, his mind does not waver.
Because he makes no distinction between sentient beings, he accomplishes all manner of various merits for them and is able to receive the full measure of all such merits.
Because he bestows kindness upon others, he does not dwell on the mind of being obstructed by their failure to repay that kindness.
This is because he has eradicated all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and provides the remedial teachings for all sentient beings;
and because, although surrounded by a great multitude, he harbors no sense of superiority.

In this way, the bodhisattva practices various deeds for the sake of both self-benefit and benefiting others, in order to accomplish the practice of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, twenty-nine phrases are subsequently taught to manifest this meaning as the merit of accomplishing the practice of the Buddha-dharma.

It should be known that such a person is like Mount Sumeru, which is immovable due to its solidity; for by relying on the non-conceptual wisdom of all supreme virtues, they cannot be moved by any conceptualization belonging to the other seven stages and so forth.
Because it relies on those dharmas, it cannot be destroyed by the mindfulness of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, owing to its firmness.

Because it relies on the practice of the Tathāgata’s internal dharma, it cannot be destroyed by those who oppose the Buddha-dharma, owing to the attainment of superior power, and because it enters into the meaning of the foremost, most profound dharma of selflessness (dharmanairātmya).
Because these persons have attained the supreme dharma of the transformation of the basis, and by relying on that dharma,
they attain supreme liberation through the extinction of afflictions.
By relying on the cultivation of the transformation of the basis, they obtain a [new] body, because the defilements of all kinds that depend upon the [old] body are extinguished.
This is because they never tire of constantly hearing the true Dharma from all the Tathāgatas;
and because, having realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no further realm to be realized that has not yet been realized, and thus they seek nothing more.
It is for the sake of expounding the True Dharma and turning the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings;
it is because his body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks and maintained in a state of sublime beauty, just as King Śakra is the object of delight for all sentient beings.
Because one has attained the ten powers of mastery within the eighth stage.

The two phrases demonstrate that in the ninth stage, one preaches the Dharma by relying on the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), maintaining correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) in accordance with all sentient beings; this meaning should be understood as explained in sequence.
This is because, in the tenth stage of a bodhisattva, the remedial dharmas have attained excellent growth, and because one has attained the removal of the obstructive dharmas that are to be remedied.
As for what is called "weak," the dharmas that are the objects of remedy are designated as weak.

Because bodhisattvas dwelling in such a state are designated as Buddhas; because although these bodhisattvas possess obstructive stages, they are free from obstruction; because these bodhisattvas surpass all other bodhisattvas dwelling in lower stages; because these bodhisattvas dwell in the equality of the bodhisattvas' peerless stage; and furthermore, because they realize the equality, single flavor, and non-self of the dharmas taught in the sūtras and so forth—both in their peerlessness and lack of distinction, and yet in their distinctness.
Because bodhisattvas dwelling in that state cannot be measured by others through discursive thought or investigation;
and because they explain all secrets with eloquence and without obstruction.
Because they are able to uphold and receive the immeasurable teachings of immeasurable Buddhas and Tathāgatas;

because they go by not going, thereby immediately receiving the great rain of Dharma through the wisdom of hearing, and subsequently entering what is to be realized through realization as it truly is.
Because they awaken to those dharmas, entering correctly and penetrating all phenomena;
because they enter the eighty-four thousand gateways of the various activities of sentient beings;
and because they apply the remedial dharmas according to those activities without weariness.
Because this bodhisattva, although seeing the world, remains detached from the world;
for the various worldly phenomena such as gain and loss, as well as the underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*) of hatred, love, greed, and anger, cannot increase within them.

Because although those bodhisattvas attain great benefits such as [the realization of] equality, they are unable to destroy or impair their portions of the various roots of goodness cultivated through practice.

Thus, as bodhisattvas cultivate and accumulate the Buddha-dharmas and correctly practice various deeds to obtain their respective superior fruits, the text next explains twenty-six phrases concerning the merit of attaining these fruits to demonstrate this meaning.

It is based on the accomplishment of non-understanding, the accomplishment of form, the accomplishment of karma, the accomplishment of the complete fulfillment of all bodhisattva stages, and the accomplishment of the ultimate entry into the Buddha stage.
This meaning should be understood according to this sequence.

It should be known that such a person attains delightful love, for they are loved by all who possess wisdom; because this bodhisattva has realized the truths as they truly are, they are therefore revered by their companions out of affectionate regard in their hearts.

Because one relies on the words of the Dharma and relies on the understanding of the characteristics of the Dharma, one knows that those teachings are weighty and thus makes offerings to them, as explained in sequence.
This is because those who respect the Buddha’s Dharma are able to make offerings.

This is because they rely on neutral persons and those who lack faith in the Buddha-dharma, and because they see that bodhisattva performing great and superior deeds, such as taking refuge in and prostrating to him.
Because they advance toward the ultimate cultivation of the bodhisattva practices, and because other bodhisattvas also make offerings to this bodhisattva.

Although those of the other two vehicles may advance and attain their respective paths, this bodhisattva possesses superior merit; thus, those followers of the two vehicles seek this merit from him, as this bodhisattva relies upon those superior practices and does not seek the Lesser Vehicle.
This is the mark of the merit of attaining the fruit through the accomplishment of the mind.

It should be known that such a person is free from deceit; because they are untainted by the qualities of deceit, they have abandoned all forms of deceit associated with worldly conditioned phenomena.

Because he is able to generate worldly joy through all his modes of conduct—coming, going, sitting, and lying down; because he has perfected his exquisite complexion and physical form from head to toe; because his majesty is so complete that he inspires respect among all the world; because his body is endowed with the thirty-two marks; and because those eighty minor characteristics of a bodhisattva are manifested in every variety of his physical appearance.
This is the mark of the merit of attaining the fruit through the accomplishment of form.
It is the mark of the merit of attaining the fruit through the accomplishment of the activity of sustaining [the teachings] based on the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Those Buddhas who see this person do so because all Buddhas perceive directly, because [this person] is the very merit of those Buddhas, and because they see according to reality.
This is because they have attained the direct vision of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; because they have attained the station of receiving the empowerment of immeasurable realized dharmas;

and because they have attained the dharmakṣāntis (patiences) of the lower, middle, and superior grades. Regarding these, the lower patience is said to exist within the seventh bhūmi; the middle patience, within the eighth and ninth bhūmis; and the superior patience, within the tenth bhūmi.
This is the mark of the merit of attaining the fruit through the complete and perfect accomplishment of the Bodhisattva stages.

That person fulfills the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) because they have realized that all aspects and all merits are fully satisfied. That person is able to subdue the various Māras; furthermore, that person is able to perform the deeds performed by a Buddha—this should be understood as the sequence of benefiting sentient beings based upon such subduing of the Māras.
This is the mark of the merit of attaining the fruit through the accomplishment of entering the Buddha-ground.
Regarding "not being startled" and so forth: what is meant by being startled?
It is called being startled because, upon hearing the profound Dharma, one considers it to be a heterodox path.
Because of that initial alarm, it becomes further intensified and continues without interruption; this is called "increased alarm.
When this alarm persists without cessation and is coupled with attachment, it is called "supreme alarm."

Because they have fallen into a state of alarm and fear, because they remain in a state of alarm and fear, and because they fear the absence of objects, it should be understood that, in this sequence, such a person does not become alarmed, does not become intensely alarmed, and does not become supremely alarmed. This is the meaning to be known.

Regarding the statement that his merits are inexhaustible: this is because the various distinctions among the seven kinds of merits resulting from practicing according to the teaching are incalculable.
As for the Buddha’s *bodhi*, as previously stated, because that *bodhi* is difficult to know, the two phrases "difficult to see" and "difficult to awaken to" are presented as a demonstration.
By means of supramundane wisdom, one attains the sphere of wisdom based on supramundane wisdom, for other mundane wisdoms cannot know that sphere.

As for "being able to believe," it refers to relying upon [the teaching] to receive, uphold, recite, explain, and personally practice in accordance with the Dharma as taught; because one does this so that others may come to know it, it is called "belief."
It should be understood that this refers to the skillful means of wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) that causes others to practice according to reality.
The merits of such acts as faith, acceptance, upholding, reciting, and explaining are immeasurable, for they constitute the domain of omniscience (*sarvajña-viṣaya*).
Next, based on the fact that even Brahmā cannot fully comprehend his perfect wisdom, as the sutra says:
"At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Great Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying: 'Brahmā!'"
"You have but a small portion of knowledge regarding the physical forms and merits of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, yet you praise them.
For what reason is this said?

It is because it is based on praise, based on merit, and based on the actual facts; thus, it is spoken in accordance with the profound meaning in this sequence. That is to say, one should understand that within the meaning, the phrases, and the words, there is profundity.
This demonstrates the knowledge of the destination toward which they are proceeding, because it involves knowing their profound intention. In what sense?
Knowing the profound intention means knowing the intention of the speaker who preaches the Dharma.
Because it manifests the dharma that accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one should understand the correspondence between the preceding and subsequent meanings and dharmas.
This is because it does not follow the literal meaning of the words, because it relies on the meaning rather than the letter, and because it relies on correct questioning and correct speech.
Because it is taught as the practice of the five powers, the verbal expression of these five powers is called "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*); this meaning should be understood.
Regarding these five powers, why are they called "powers"?
Because they are associated with four kinds of power. What are these four?
First is the power of sustaining the deeds performed by the Buddha;
Second is the power to subdue all non-Buddhists;
third is the power to know all demonic activities, and having known them, to be able to distance oneself from their influence;
fourth is the power to ultimately attain the three vehicles.
Within those dharmas, each is in accordance [with the others], because the Tathāgata, relying on those dharmas, is able to teach them in excellent accord.
These five powers are taught based on the five kinds of profundity.
What are the five? First, profundity based on characteristics;
second, profundity based on intentionality.
Third is the profundity based on time and place;
fourth is the profundity based on progressive attainment;
fifth is the profundity based on the constant teaching of the Dharma in accordance with [the needs of beings].
In this sequence, regarding profundity by way of characteristics: because the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena across the three periods of time are difficult to realize.
Phenomena of the past and so forth are explained by means of four modes:
First, speaking based on phenomena;
second, speaking based on specific antidotes;
third, speaking based on the meaning of conventional truth.
Fourth is the explanation based on the distinction of the vehicles for those who progress.
What is the meaning of this?
Regarding the explanation based on phenomena, it means that the phenomena of the three times are explained by means of the characteristics of the phenomena of the three times.
Regarding the matters of the three periods of time—namely the past, future, and present—this is what is called the "prediction concerning the three periods of time.
Because one speaks of the matters of the three periods of time by relying on the Tathāgata’s unobstructed wisdom, it is termed the "prediction concerning the three periods of time."

Regarding the explanation based on the relationship between the object of treatment and its antidote: the afflictions to be treated are defiled, while the dharmas that act as antidotes are pure; furthermore, those afflictions are distinguished by two types, namely the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Wholesome dharmas also have two kinds of distinctions, namely the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
The mundane further has two kinds of distinctions, namely the distinction between the tainted and the untainted.
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) also has two kinds of distinctions, namely the distinction between that which is faulty and that which is faultless.
The faultless also has two kinds of distinctions, namely the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding the explanation according to the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): it is because one explains the distinct characteristics of the self, sentient beings, and so forth by relying on provisional names and designations.

Regarding the explanation according to the distinction of the progressive vehicles: it is because one attains the realization of true suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), based upon purity.
Just as one realizes [the truth] in successive stages, so too does one advance toward and take hold of both the mundane world and nirvāṇa. What does this clarify?
That which ordinary people advance toward and take hold of is precisely the mundane world.
The followers of the two vehicles grasp the realization of the dharmas of other stages as *nirvāṇa*, because they take the limit of quiescence as their *nirvāṇa*;
whereas the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not abide in either of these two states.
For those who possess the first power, because they are free from the fault of attachment, the analogies of illusions and so forth are taught.
What does this clarify?
Just as the bodies of elephants and other forms produced by illusion are not established as real, so too the bodies of all phenomena such as form, which are expressed by words, are not established.
Just as one might dream within a dream of experiencing various objects, yet those various objects within the dream are due to inversion;

so too, because the dharmas and meanings employed in such verbal expressions and the gateways for experiencing the joy of the Dharma are merely false conceptualizations, these verbal expressions and sounds of the teaching exist like echoes—uttering words within the midst of empty space without any place of abiding. Thus, the sounds and voices of the Dharma teaching abide nowhere, yet they are perfectly established within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

It is just as when a reflection appears: although one sees only its marks, and though one sees various forms and appearances that seem to possess color, those various forms and appearances are not in actual association with the substance of that phenomenon.

And based on those dharmas, such speech arises in accordance with them, stating that all dharmas are likewise merely signs (*nimitta*). Although there are various distinctions of names, the dharma expressed by these names collectively is not [inherently] associated with them, because it arises in accordance with the signs of those dharmas.

Just as when one seals clay or similar material with various seals and sees a second seal [impressed upon it], yet the substance of the original seals does not shift or enter [the clay], so too are all phenomena seen and described in such words.

Although one hears the distinct characteristics and differences of objects such as form through the medium of language, these linguistic expressions do not reside within the phenomena or their meanings, yet they are heard in this way.

Just as a mirage has no actual substance of water yet water is seen therein, so too, while language speaks of all phenomena, the essential nature and characteristics of those phenomena do not exist as they are described, yet those various phenomena are nonetheless perceived.

Just as that space is originally unborn and originally unceasing, and although one speaks of space by means of words, that space has no essence that can be spoken of; likewise, when words speak of the meaning of phenomena (*dharma*), because the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) has no essence that can be spoken of, and because all phenomena lack any such words by which they could be expressed, thus in teaching the Dharma there is not a single thing taught, for that teaching of the Dharma is like an illusion and so forth.
Therefore, it is demonstrated through metaphors such as illusions.
Thus, not being attached to the words, teachings, or meanings, and attaining the joy of unimpeded wisdom and eloquence—this is called benefit; this meaning should be understood.
What is the meaning clarified here?
All verbal dharmas are spoken without departing from the dharma-realm and are spoken without differentiating the dharma-realm.
What is the meaning of this?

All teachings on the distinctions of form and so forth do not depart from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because they teach the harmony of the dharma-realm and because they teach the distinctions among all phenomena such as form without attachment.

Regarding "relying on the profound intention": one should understand that this means being able to know the Tathāgata’s profound intention by relying on the six kinds of intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of the Tathāgata.
What are these six kinds of intentional terminology?
First, the intentional meaning regarding mindfulness;
second, the intentional meaning regarding non-explanation;
third, the intentional meaning regarding specific remedies.
Fourth is the intentional meaning regarding phenomena;
fifth is the intentional meaning regarding the mind;
sixth is the intentional meaning regarding the transformation of syllables.
“Brahmā! The Tathāgata may speak of defiled phenomena as pure,” and so forth; this demonstrates the intentional meaning (*abhiprāya*) of mindfulness.
What is the significance of this?

Because one does not perceive the essence of the defiled phenomena of affliction; because one firmly clings to the essence of pure phenomena; and because there is no essence to either the defilement or the purity of right mindfulness.

Because one unswervingly clings to this as the essential characteristic of defiled phenomena; because the mind unswervingly clings to this as the essential characteristic of pure phenomena; and because although those defiled phenomena are not right mindfulness, those defiled phenomena do not constitute [true] defiled phenomena—this is called the Tathāgata’s intentional terminology regarding mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
"Furthermore, Brahmā!
By relying on giving, I demonstrate nirvāṇa," and so forth; this demonstrates the underlying intention (saṃdhi) of non-explanation.
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha teaches all phenomena with a mind free from conceptual arising.

Since all phenomena lack such power as to be able to transmigrate from this world to another, and since my teaching holds that phenomena have no intrinsic substance, there is not a single phenomenon that can undergo transmigration.
For this reason, not even a single hair’s breadth of a dharma transmigrates to another world.
Therefore, to claim that one attains nirvana based on the act of giving is impossible.
This is called the Tathāgata’s intentional terminology regarding non-explanation.
"Manifesting nirvāṇa through [the practice of] ethical discipline up to wisdom"—what does this clarify?
This clarifies the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) regarding the respective remedies. What is the meaning of this?

Because one abandons the dharmas to be countered, such as the violation of precepts, and practices the joyful conduct of the *pāramitās*, the observance of the precepts and so forth is called "nirvāṇa.

Because one abandons the afflictions that give rise to the breaking of precepts, the body, speech, and mind do not engage in unwholesome conduct; because one is free from all intent to harm, relying on the emptiness of that harmful mind; because one no longer gives rise to a mind of patience [toward wrongdoing]; and because one is free from indolence, constantly cultivating diligence for the increase of the wholesome and the destruction of unwholesome conduct, yet lacks such a [self-referential] mind;
and because one acts for the sake of increasing the wholesome and destroying unwholesome conduct, yet lacks such a [self-referential] mind.
Furthermore, because there is no further movement of the mind, and because there is no applied or sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
What is the meaning of this?
It is because one is free from all movement of the mind, and because there is no distracted mind of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Because one is detached from all perceived objects, the thought "I have attained the mind" does not arise; it is called "attainment" precisely because there is nothing to be attained, for no phenomena are perceived.
This is called the Tathāgata’s intentional terminology regarding specific antidotes.

“Lust is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the dharma-nature because it lacks the characteristic of desire,” and so on, up to “delusion is the reality-limit of the dharma-nature because it is without delusion; for within true suchness (tathatā), there is no reality-limit of lust and so forth, as they are non-existent. This demonstrates the intentional terminology regarding phenomena (dharma).
What does this clarify?
Because the *dharmatā* of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is devoid of the characteristic of delusion, this demonstrates the underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) of the Dharma.
What is the meaning of this?
One should understand this meaning: because apart from *tathatā* (suchness), no phenomena such as greed or the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) can be spoken of.
This is called the Tathāgata’s intentional terminology regarding the Dharma (*dharmasaṃdhāyabhāṣita*).

The statement, "Because the world is nirvāṇa—being neither subject to decline nor birth—and even falsehood is true speech, it is for the sake of those with overweening pride," demonstrates the intentional terminology regarding the mind (*cittasaṃdhāyabhāṣita*).
What is the meaning of this?
It is because understanding that the world is fundamentally unarisen and fundamentally unceasing is itself nirvāṇa.
To grasp at nirvāṇa as having a substantial body and to thus apprehend its characteristics—this mental error is precisely the world.
Those who speak of reality do so by relying on the gateway of verbal expression; yet if one perceives this as reality, it is itself false.
Those who speak of falsity are people of pride who, through false discrimination, take that which is unreal to be real, thereby grasping at the true mark while failing to realize its unreality.
This is called the Tathāgata’s intentional meaning regarding the mind.

Furthermore, Brahmā, because the Tathāgata acts according to his will, he may himself say, "I am one who teaches the extreme of permanence," and so forth; this demonstrates the intentional meaning regarding the transformation of syllables.

For what reason? Because it is taught that nirvāṇa and so forth are eternal dharmas; because it is taught that there are various defiled dharmas such as the afflictions; because it is taught that one severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions such as craving; because it is taught that there is no performance of unwholesome conduct; because it is taught that there is no karma of body and so forth; because one perceives all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and false views; because omniscience does not follow other causes and conditions; because one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma-realm of nirvāṇa; because one is not bound by birth or non-birth within any realm of existence due to not relying on karma and afflictions; because one has attained the ultimate severance of craving and karma; and because one does not dwell in the triple world and does not belong to the triple world.
As the sutra states, "The Tathāgata does not possess such things as these.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that the Tathāgata is free from views such as the extreme of eternalism and the like, or impermanence and the like.
Furthermore, as for the statement that such things do not exist, it is because within the Buddha-dharma there is no such teaching, and what is thus taught cannot be perceived.
"Brahmā, you should know that this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his own will."
Regarding the question, "By relying on what intention can arrogant sentient beings abandon their pride?"—what meaning does this clarify?
It demonstrates that within the teachings previously explained, there is an attachment to divergent meanings; for as is the case with names, so it is with meanings as well.

"Brahmā! If a bodhisattva knows that the Tathāgata speaks according to the skillful means of following [the capacities of beings]," this is stated next below, based on being free from such attachment to names and meanings.
By what meaning is this so?
Because within the teaching of the Dharma there are two kinds of practice:
first, the practice of syllables; [second, the practice of meaning].
Second is the practice of meaning.
What does this clarify?
It means that such names proceed within the meaning, and such meanings proceed within the names; this is the profound intent of the Tathāgata.
Based on this profound intent, one should understand that the characteristics of skillful means, the meaning of the syllables, and the wisdom of practice are thus well-known.
This practice is called "practice" (*caryā*) because the bodhisattva advances toward and attains the practice of his own will.

According to the profound meaning thus explained, because skillful means gather all phenomena, one is able to thoroughly understand the various phenomena spoken of in all teachings; therefore, a bodhisattva should be known as one who is neither startled nor terrified by any of the Buddhas' verbal expressions, sounds, or voices when they preach the Dharma.
Because sentient beings follow various states of mind, the Bodhisattva relies upon those skillful means to enable them to believe and accept [the teachings].

Whether hearing that a Buddha has appeared in the world or has not appeared in the world, he manifests each instance—such as appearing or not appearing—in diverse ways. Without grasping or attachment, he employs skillful means to cause those sentient beings to believe and enter into all dharmas.

Because the bodies of sentient beings who are to be converted have not yet reached full maturity, he teaches them shallow dharmas, relying on pleasure and manifesting pleasure, in order to bring those beings' bodies to maturity;
once their bodies have matured through experiencing pleasure, he then teaches them the profound dharmas.
Therefore, one should understand that the teaching of the Dharma proceeds according to sequence and timing.
How should this be understood?
First, one should teach the coarse and shallow Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies the inclusion of cause and effect; the inclusion of that contemplation; and the inclusion of that activity.
Furthermore, it clarifies the inclusion of sentient beings through the skillful means of teaching and transforming them; the inclusion of practice; and the inclusion of the fruit of practice.

The statement that "through giving one attains great wealth, up to and including through wisdom one abandons all afflictions" refers to the grasping of cause and effect based on the practice of wholesome dharmas.
Patience serves as the antidote to ugliness, because patience can give rise to a joyful mind and because patience can act as the cause for physical beauty.

Because one diligently cultivates various practices through the wisdom derived from hearing and so forth, they can serve as the cause for knowledge; because one transcends the suffering of suffering and its causes;
because one can abandon all afflictions by observing them as they truly are with wisdom; and because the causes of all afflictions are dispersed and extinguished, no longer accumulating.
Furthermore, regarding this practice of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) which cultivates the contemplation of wholesome dharmas, what is the cause of that contemplation?
It is because one takes the wisdom of extensive learning as the means to encompass that contemplation; thus, one grasps that contemplation.

One practices the conduct of the body and so forth, embracing the ten paths of wholesome action; because one relies on these ten types of karma to achieve all merits among gods and humans, one embraces that karma.
The immeasurable grasping of activity is for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings; it is through the skillful means of teaching and transforming that one grasps sentient beings.

Regarding the skillful means of bringing sentient beings to maturity, one relies upon *śamatha* to cultivate all wholesome dharmas; thus, because one attains *vipaśyanā* by means of practicing *śamatha*, this constitutes the grasping of practice.
Because one attains the nirvana of the three vehicles by relying on the three vehicles, this refers to the inclusion of the fruits of practice.

Because practices such as begging for alms, having few desires, and the dhūta austerities bring only slight benefit to sentient beings and do not enable the preaching of the Dharma, they are excluded.
In order to cause sentient beings to enter [the path] by following along with it, the Tathāgata speaks such shallow teachings first, and only thereafter does he speak the profound teaching.
What meaning does this clarify?

He teaches coarse and superficial dharmas to clarify cause and effect for the sake of those disciples whose faculties are not yet matured, and for those beings who perceive the matter of cause and effect through their own minds; he thereby gathers in those who hold views of a self characterized by the notions of agent and action.

Therefore, having clarified cause and effect, the Tathāgata next explains the remedies—the counteracting and the countered—to demonstrate that his own person is free from those false views, for the Tathāgata truly does not perceive a self, a sentient being, a life-span, or a person.
What is the meaning of this?
The meanings of a self (*ātman*), a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-span (*āyus*), and a person (*puruṣa*) should be understood as previously explained.

Because one does not perceive those dharmas of cause and effect consisting of the remedial and the remediated, it is briefly stated that one relies on and follows worldly retribution: because one does not perceive the receiving of retribution for giving and so forth; because one does not perceive the non-receiving of retribution for stinginess and so forth; because one has attained the removal of the dharmas of practice consisting of the remedial and the remediated; and because one does not perceive the existence or non-existence of the marks of the fruit of nirvāṇa apart from the fruit of the world.

"Brahmā! The Tathāgata constantly teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, and these sentient beings rely upon the Tathāgata’s instructions, practicing exactly as taught according to reality and diligently cultivating various practices. For what purpose do they practice and diligently perform those deeds, such that they do not even attain nirvāṇa and do not perceive nirvāṇa? What meaning does this clarify?

As when the Dharma is taught in a superficial manner, sentient beings grasp at it and perceive the various characteristics of phenomena; likewise, although they practice for the sake of supramundane fruits, they do not perceive those fruits. The Tathāgata manifests such teaching of the Dharma as being the cause of the mundane world.
What is the meaning of this?
For one who practices in reliance upon the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, this constitutes the fundamental conformity to wholesome dharmas.
The phrase "practicing various [spiritual] disciplines" is an explanation, because it is taught sequentially based on not apprehending dharmas and not seeing dharmas.
"One who does not attain the Dharma" means that through the observation of wisdom, one is unable to attain it.
"One who does not see the Dharma" means that with the body alone, one cannot realize nirvāṇa.
What is the meaning clarified by the phrase "in order to cause sentient beings to grasp the sublime Dharma"?

He teaches both shallow and profound doctrines in order to lead sentient beings into these two types of teachings—the shallow and the profound—and to manifest the entry into the characteristics of the Dharma.
What is the meaning of this?
Those who enter the Dharma do so by means of four types of entry.
It should be understood that for the sake of sentient beings who are to be converted, he manifests liberation in order to lead them to realize that Dharma. This is the meaning to be known.
The four kinds of entry are: entry by means of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), practice (*caryā*), teaching (*deśanā*), and attainment (*prāpti*).

Because the various faculties such as the eye are devoid of the two characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to self" and are empty of essence, once one has understood those characteristics, they can no longer deceive; because one thereby attains entry into liberation, it is called "entry by means of characteristics."
By relying on the characteristics of the eye and so forth, one is able to enter liberation; therefore, these are called the "characteristics for entering liberation.

Thus, because one practices correctly within those characteristics of emptiness, one attains entry into liberation. Being undeceived by characteristics is the opposite of being deceived; for this reason, one enters by means of cultivation.

It explains the characteristics through which all sentient beings enter liberation; therefore, based on these two factors—characteristics and practice—it demonstrates the remedies for the defilements of karma and afflictions, as well as the defilements of birth and so forth.
Regarding the gates such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), what meaning does this clarify?

It clarifies that these are the remedial dharmas (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) which counteract the afflictions of views, characteristics, aspirations, and karmic defilements, as well as the defilements of birth and so forth.
What does this clarify?
By means of the gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), one counteracts the defilement of karma and the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*).
By means of the gate of non-practice (*apravṛtti*), one counters saṃsāra; thus, it counteracts the defilement of birth.
Regarding the gate of non-arising and non-ceasing, what meaning does this clarify?
It clarifies that within the very midst of those differentiated phenomena of arising and defilement, there is an antidote;

and that for those very objects of treatment, there is further an antidote. By means of the gate of neither coming from anywhere nor going anywhere, there is yet another antidote; and by means of the gate of neither retreating nor departing, one enters the characteristic of liberation, following that sequence.
Regarding the gate of the tranquility of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*): what meaning does this clarify?
It clarifies that those phenomena recede from their own intrinsic stillness.
What meaning does it demonstrate?
It is because it manifests that all those defilements are utterly quiescent.
For what reason is it said to be "quiescent by nature"?
It is because one enters the Dharma by relying on the purity of its intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-viśuddhi*).
Therefore, it is subsequently stated: "Furthermore, Brahmā!
The Tathāgata demonstrates all names as gateways to liberation," and so forth.
What is the meaning of this?
This is because they are successively shared yet lack mutual correspondence, and because their intrinsic nature is inert.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because distinct names are assigned based on distinct phenomena, and because the preceding and succeeding syllables of these various names do not reach one another.
Furthermore, there is another distinction: because the meaning [of reality] and words do not reach one another.
What is the meaning clarified by such a statement?
It is that among all phenomena, there is no such language by which they can be expressed.
Having thus spoken in accordance with the dharma-characteristics that are beyond words and names, the Tathāgata manifests all words and names, for he teaches that they are the cause of liberation.
What does this clarify? It clarifies the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Having taught the Dharma according to reality as it is, how is liberation attained?
Therefore, it is said next: "Brahmā!
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that is defiled.
What does this clarify?

Having taught the Dharma in a simple manner for those whose faculties are immature, he speaks of the gates of entry into the Dharma as the causes and conditions for severing all afflictions and defiled dharmas in accordance with their needs; thus, within all the teachings he has expounded, he reveals the gate of liberation.
What meaning does this manifestation demonstrate?
It demonstrates *nirvāṇa*. What meaning does this [subsequent] manifestation demonstrate?
Regarding the remaining afflictions of those in training who have seen the truths, it is shown that such practitioners attain liberation by being free from those afflictions.
For those who have not yet seen the true reality, he teaches the Dharma through skillful means to lead them into the equality of all phenomena—the true suchness—and manifests nirvana for their sake.
There are two meanings by which one should understand great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):
first, the ultimate remedy for those phenomena that are to be remedied;
second, the mind of great compassion in all its aspects.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that by being far removed from all dharmas to be abandoned and by being free from all habitual tendencies and afflictions, one attains the body of a Tathāgata.
Because all aspects [of omniscience] have been attained, this is briefly explained by way of four kinds of great compassionate mind:

first, the great compassionate mind associated with detachment; second, the great compassionate mind associated with [practice]; third, the great compassionate mind associated with maturation; and fourth, the great compassionate mind associated with non-abiding.
The third refers to the mind of great compassion;
the fourth refers to the practice of the mind of great compassion.
As for "separation from association," it is because consciousness is separated from consciousness and thus does not associate, whereas it associates with the mind that perceives a self and so forth.
What does this demonstrate?
It demonstrates the mind that is dissociated from great compassion and the mind that is associated with great compassion.

Thus, in sequence, all phenomena are without self (*anātman*), up to all phenomena being without a person (*puruṣa*). Based on the teaching of the non-self of persons, it is said that all phenomena are non-existent; based on the teaching of the non-self of phenomena, it is said that those two [types of non-self] are themselves [non-existent].
The absence of the mark of self in persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the absence of the mark of self in phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is called "non-abiding.
To speak of non-abiding means that because one does not cling to the essence of any phenomena, one does not dwell in any phenomena; this is how it should be understood.
What does this clarify?
That which is called "abiding" refers to abiding within the sense bases (*āyatana*), for one abides in those places by means of the gateway of self-view and craving.
Now, that which has no abiding has no place of refuge; if there is no place of refuge, how can there be a refuge?

Because they return to the three realms and return to the six destinies; because they depend on those entries to assume a body, because they are born from them, and because they are constantly submerged within them.
What is called "sinking" is due to the notions of "I" and "mine. Because one takes birth in various places as a body, and because the thought of "I" arises, there is birth.
For one who has no place of refuge, there is no notion of "I"; for one who has no notion of "I," there is no notion of "mine."
Those who have a place of refuge become attached to the notion of a self; those who are attached to a self possess the notion of "mine.
Because those who are attached to "mine" falsely discriminate that the self is predominant—even though all phenomena are equal and shared by all—sentient beings thus give rise to such delusions.
What does this clarify?
It refers to grasping and attachment based on things.

"Based on things" means being dependent upon fields, houses, gardens, and so forth; being dependent upon parents, wives, children, and so forth; and being dependent upon clothing, food and drink, bedding, and so forth.
Regarding "appropriation," it refers to the appropriation of all objects of enjoyment.
Regarding "clinging," it refers to clinging to them as one's own property, because one considers fields, houses, and so forth to belong specifically to oneself.
Thus, there is attachment to birth and attachment to passing away from birth.

Regarding "attachment to birth," it means that one goes from this place to another place due to the act of grasping; because of this grasping, the defilements of karma and afflictions increase and become all-pervasive.

Because they arise, depart, and produce defilement throughout time and place, they depend on the three types of entanglements—greed, hatred, and delusion—and are defiled according to what they defile.
What is the meaning of this?
Regarding the statement that greed, hatred, and delusion are defiled according to what they defile: for what reason are these two [categories] designated as depending on fundamental defilement?

This refers to how [the continuity] comes from the past life to this life, and from this life proceeds toward that life; taking this as the primary principle, it is thus described and thus manifested, such that in life after life and birth after birth there is an uninterrupted succession, performing its various functions.
Sentient beings are born in this manner, revolving incessantly from one state to another; they study various arts and engage in various occupations.
Possessing the marks of masculine vigor, they perform all conditioned phenomena of conceptual proliferation, accumulating objects and experiencing those objects.
Sentient beings engage in such false conceptualizations;
all of these should be understood as belonging to the category of worldly persons.

Furthermore, there is another category based on those who have left the household life, namely, the characteristics of wrong views held by non-Buddhists and the aspirations associated with those wrong views.
What does this clarify?
"False view" refers to views such as [the belief in] a self (*ātman*).
What is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the false conceptualization of various objective characteristics.
As for what is called "vow," it refers to the mind constantly delighting in seeking birth in the world and so forth.
One should understand that this means: as previously explained, there is the manifestation of a mind that is either devoid of compassion or not devoid of compassion. This is the intended meaning.

For those whose minds are either detached or undetached from such states, he teaches the practice of the Dharma; because they rely on the quest for sensual desire, the quest for existence, or the quest for the holy life—these being the inverted paths—he teaches the practice of compassion as the remedy for those [afflictions] that are to be countered. Thus, he next explains the practice of compassion.
What does this clarify?
Those who rely on the perverted path of craving engage in mutual strife because of their grasping.
For the sake of various desires, they fight among themselves, even with their own parents, wives, children, and so forth.
This sequence follows from faults such as malice, resentment, and contention.
For those who follow the perverted path through the pursuit of existence, there is association with perversion.

Because they seek Brahmā and so forth through the perversion of eternalism, and because they grasp perversely, it is called "perversion. For those who are thus perverted, [the teaching] causes them to leave the perverted path and enter the non-perverted path.

Furthermore, because those who rely on the perverted path of seeking existence abide in heterodox paths, it is impossible to teach and transform those sentient beings of heterodox paths so that they might enter the true path.
Regarding those who seek the path of perversity while relying on the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there are briefly three types: namely, not seeking, seeking wrongly, and seeking base things.
What is the meaning of this?

Because all the world suffers from the fault of lack of self-mastery, the fault of wrong livelihood, and the fault of appearing as a friend, and because they are defiled by the karma of various afflictions and the phenomena of suffering—being householders who delight in the domestic life—sentient beings do not seek the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Because those who do not seek the holy life do not seek the path to liberation, this is what is called stinginess and being overwhelmed by stinginess, as well as the habitual tendencies of greed, deception, and indolence; these are to be extracted one by one in successive order.

Those who do not know contentment and seize the wealth of others do so because they seek their own livelihood through unrighteous means; thus, their practice of giving and other virtues is insufficient.
That sentient beings constantly act as servants for the sake of wealth, houses, wives, children, and affectionate ties is shown to demonstrate that their minds lack self-mastery.
Regarding those who conceive the notion of solidity toward these fragile and unsubstantial things, it is because they perceive permanence within impermanent requisites for life and so forth.
What is the meaning of "making offerings and showing respect"?
Because they are bound by food and drink and thus fail to achieve accomplishment,
although sentient beings may claim such persons are spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), these sentient beings are actually evil associates (*pāpamitra*), for they manifest as enemies.
Those who live by wrong livelihood do so by deceiving others through the use of false scales and measures.
Furthermore, while one can only ultimately attain great enlightenment by diligently cultivating all practices among all dharmas, those sentient beings are characterized by indolence and weariness.
The most supreme state of liberation attained by the Noble Ones is not something obtained by practitioners through inverted causes;
yet sentient beings, seeking false brahmacarya, cultivate various practices based on inverted causes.
Those who ought to attain [liberation] instead seek the liberation of non-Buddhist outsiders; this is so that they may not practice those false paths. Why is this?
Because they do not attain the liberation of the noble ones.
Regarding the phrase "sentient beings abandon the supreme Great Vehicle and its unimpeded [qualities]," it is because they seek inferior brahmacarya;
that is, they abandon the unsurpassed, foremost Great Vehicle and instead seek the lower-tier teachings of the Small Vehicle.
